title: What If Your Standards Aren’t High? What If Your Pride Just Learned Better Vocabulary?
paragraphs: What If Your Standards Aren’t High? What If Your Pride Just Learned Better Vocabulary?

There is a kind of pride that no longer brags, shouts, or demands attention. It calls itself discernment. It calls itself standards. It calls itself maturity. And sometimes, while we are congratulating ourselves for having “grown,” Jesus is exposing something far less flattering beneath the vocabulary.
What if the thing you have been calling “standards” is sometimes just a respectable way of deciding who is beneath you?
That question is uncomfortable.
Especially because standards are not inherently wrong.

Discernment is biblical. Wisdom matters. Character matters. Boundaries can be necessary. Scripture never commands you to trust everybody, date everybody, marry everybody, employ everybody, remain close friends with everybody, or give unlimited access to people who repeatedly demonstrate destructive behavior.
Jesus Himself said, “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment” (John 7:24).
So this is not an argument for becoming naïve.
It is an invitation to ask a much more dangerous question:
Can I recognize what is wrong in someone without beginning to believe I am worth more than they are?
Because somewhere between discernment and disgust, between wisdom and superiority, between recognizing sin and despising the sinner...
pride can quietly change clothes.
And respectable pride is especially dangerous because it rarely introduces itself as pride.
It says:
“I just know my worth.”
“I protect my peace.”
“I have standards now.”
“I can read people.”
“I don't associate with people like that anymore.”
“They're not on my level.”
“I've outgrown them.”
Some of those sentences can describe legitimate boundaries.
But they can also hide something ugly.
Contempt.
And contempt can wear very clean clothes.
It can carry a Bible.
It can know theology.
It can quote sermons.
It can talk about “discernment.”
It can post about protecting its peace while secretly enjoying the feeling of being morally, intellectually, financially, socially, or spiritually above somebody else.
Then Philippians 2 walks into the room.
And suddenly there is nowhere comfortable for our ego to sit.
Paul writes:
“Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.”
Philippians 2:3.
One Greek word deserves to stop us:
κενοδοξίαν — kenodoxian.
It carries the idea of empty glory, vain conceit, an inflated concern with one's own importance.
Empty glory.
That is terrifying because pride does not require you to stand in front of a mirror saying, “I am amazing.”
Sometimes pride only needs you to look at another person and quietly think:
“At least I'm not like them.”
Jesus already told a story about somebody who prayed like that.
A Pharisee stood before God and thanked Him that he was not like other people.
A tax collector, meanwhile, could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
His prayer was essentially:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
Jesus said it was the broken man who went home justified rather than the self-satisfied religious man.
That is Luke 18:9–14.
And notice how Luke introduces the parable.
Jesus told it to people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt.”
There it is.
Not merely righteousness.
Not merely standards.
Contempt.
That is where the heart gets exposed.
Because biblical discernment can say, “What you're doing is wrong,” without saying, “Therefore, I am better than you.”
Biblical wisdom can establish a boundary without requiring hatred.
Biblical holiness can refuse participation in sin without forgetting that the sinner is still an image-bearer desperately needing the same Savior we desperately need.
You can walk away without looking down.
You can say no without sneering.
You can recognize someone's immaturity without worshiping your own maturity.
You can refuse a relationship without dehumanizing the person you refused.
You can identify false teaching without secretly enjoying the destruction of the false teacher.
You can confront sin while remembering the frightening sentence:
“But for the grace of God...”
Maybe that is where some of us have drifted.
We remember what people did to us, but forget what Christ forgave in us.
We remember their weakness, but forget ours.
We notice how far they still have to go while conveniently forgetting how far Jesus carried us.
And grace becomes something we celebrate when describing our own story...
but ration when describing somebody else's.
Read the next words of Philippians.
“Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.”
Then Paul does something devastating.
He does not merely tell us to become nicer.
He points us to Jesus.
“τοῦτο φρονεῖτε ἐν ὑμῖν ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
“Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.”
Philippians 2:5.
Τοῦτο φρονεῖτε — touto phroneite.
Think this way.
Adopt this disposition.
Let this mindset shape you.
And whose mindset?
Not the mindset of the person with the strongest boundaries.
Not the person with the most impressive accomplishments.
Not the person with the cleanest reputation.
Not the person who has finally “leveled up.”
Jesus Christ.
And what does Paul immediately tell us about Him?

Christ, though existing in the form of God, did not exploit His equality with God for His own advantage, but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
The One who actually had every reason to be above us...
came down.
Think about that.
We spend so much energy climbing imaginary ladders above other sinners while the Lord of glory descended toward them.
We build status.
Jesus took the servant's place.
We protect our image.
Jesus accepted public shame.
We want to be recognized.
Jesus washed feet.
We want everybody to know our value.
Jesus allowed Himself to be mocked, stripped, beaten, rejected, and crucified.
The sinless One moved toward sinners.
The Holy One touched lepers.
The King ate with people respectable religion avoided.
And when Jesus encountered broken people, He never confused compassion with approval.
He could forgive without pretending sin was harmless.
He could love without lying.
He could say to the woman caught in adultery, “Neither do I condemn you,” and also, “go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11).
Grace and truth.
Mercy and holiness.
Compassion and repentance.
Jesus never needed contempt to maintain conviction.
Neither do we.
And maybe that is the line we desperately need to recover.
Standards determine what you permit. Superiority determines how you perceive.
Those are not the same thing.
You may have a standard that prevents someone from becoming your spouse.
That does not make that person worthless.
You may establish boundaries with a manipulative family member.
That does not give you permission to nurture hatred.
You may recognize serious theological error.
That does not make cruelty a fruit of the Spirit.
You may have grown beyond behaviors that once controlled you.
That does not mean the people still trapped there are beneath you.
Remember where Jesus found you.
Maybe your chains looked different.
Maybe your scandal was hidden.
Maybe nobody saw what happened in your mind.
Maybe your addiction never became public.
Maybe your bitterness looked respectable.
Maybe your lust stayed behind a screen.
Maybe your jealousy learned to smile.
Maybe your insecurity became ambition.
Maybe your need for validation became “excellence.”
Maybe your pride learned Christian vocabulary.
But Jesus knew.
Every thought.
Every motive.
Every secret.
Every compromise.
Every night you would never want projected onto a church screen.
Every failure buried beneath your reputation.
He knew the entire unedited story.
And still...
the cross.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus did not wait until sinners became impressive enough to deserve rescue.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not once we had our lives together.
Not once we became respectable.
Not once we reached His level.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
So how strange would it be to stand beneath a bloodstained cross, forgiven entirely by mercy, and begin sorting other sinners according to how far beneath us we think they are?
There are no self-made people at Calvary.
Only sinners and a Savior.
And this does not erase wisdom.
Please understand that.
Humility does not mean returning to an abusive relationship.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean restored trust.
Love does not mean enabling destructive behavior.
Christian compassion does not require abandoning biblical convictions.
Discernment matters.
Boundaries matter.
Truth matters.
Holiness matters.
But none of those things requires contempt.
You can have standards without having a throne.
Maybe that sentence needs to stay with you.
You can have standards without having a throne.
Because the throne was never yours.
Perhaps the person irritating you today is standing in a chapter you once occupied.
Perhaps the believer you consider immature is learning lessons God patiently taught you over years.
Perhaps the person whose failures embarrass you is living publicly through the kind of battle you were fortunate enough to fight privately.
Perhaps they really are wrong.
Perhaps your discernment is completely accurate.
And perhaps your heart toward them is still sinful.
Both things can be true.
That is what makes respectable pride so difficult to detect.
You can be correct about somebody...
and wrong before God in the way you hold your correctness.
Truth without humility can become a weapon for feeding the ego.
Paul understood this.

Galatians 6:1 tells believers that when someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person “in a spirit of gentleness,” while watching themselves lest they too be tempted.
Not mock them.
Not publicly enjoy their collapse.
Not use their failure to demonstrate our superiority.
Restore them.
Gently.
While remembering:
I can fall too.
That sounds very different from the culture of public humiliation we have learned to consume.
Somebody falls, and everyone gathers.
Screenshots.
Reactions.
Comments.
Memes.
Whispers disguised as prayer requests.
And sometimes Christians participate while calling it “discernment.”
But imagine Jesus standing beside you while you talk about that person.
Would your tone change?
Would the joke still be funny?
Would you still share the screenshot?
Would you still enjoy exposing them?
Would you pray differently if you remembered that the blood you are depending upon for eternity is the same blood capable of cleansing the person you cannot stand?
This is where Christianity stops being branding and becomes crucifixion.
Not His crucifixion alone.
The death of our ego.
The death of our need to be above somebody.
The death of our addiction to comparison.
The death of that secret pleasure we experience when somebody else's failure makes our own life look cleaner.
And perhaps somebody reading this is realizing:
“I thought I was discerning. But somewhere along the way, I became proud.”
Then don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to repentance.
The Gospel does not say, “Discover how ugly your heart can be and then fix yourself.”
The Gospel says there is a Savior for proud people too.
Confess it.
Name it.
“Jesus, I have looked down on people You died to save.”
“Jesus, I have confused wisdom with superiority.”
“Jesus, I have enjoyed being right more than I have desired restoration.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And He is faithful.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Grace reaches even here.
Even into respectable pride.
Even into religious pride.
Even into the heart that learned how to hide arrogance beneath sophisticated language.
That is what Jesus does.
He rewrites people.
Scandal becomes testimony.
Condemnation meets mercy.
Pride bows.
Shame loses its final word.
The sinner discovers grace.
And the forgiven learn to look at other sinners differently.
Not because sin suddenly stops mattering.
But because the cross reminds us that we needed rescue too.
So before you say someone is beneath your standards, ask yourself something harder:
Do my standards protect obedience to God...
or protect my sense of superiority?
When I establish boundaries, do I grieve for the person...
or secretly enjoy feeling above them?
When somebody falls, do I pray for restoration...
or become energized by the scandal?
When I notice someone's weakness, does it move me toward compassion...
or comparison?
When I say, “I know my worth,” do I mean my worth in Christ...
or have I begun using human beings as measuring sticks for my ego?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If God exposed something while you were reading this, don't turn the moment into shame. Turn it into surrender.
Somebody quietly fighting the same battle may need to know transformation is possible.
Not as a badge saying, “I know somebody who needs this.”
Share it first as a confession:
“I need this too.”
Leave changed.
Go back to Philippians 2.
Look again at Jesus.
The highest One descended.
The Holy One served.
The innocent One carried the cross.
The King humbled Himself.
And the Savior who had every right to condemn us chose to rescue everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
So keep your biblical convictions.
Keep wise boundaries.
Exercise discernment.
Pursue holiness.
But surrender the throne.
Because when grace has truly brought you to your knees at the foot of the cross, it becomes increasingly difficult to look down on somebody else.
You may have every reason to walk away from someone's behavior—but never forget that Jesus once walked toward a sinner like you.
